title: Build a small Mithila study from repeated lines and filled spaces
description: Study how a Mithila artist organizes a small scene with repeated linework, flat color and filled spaces, then make an original composition under the artist’s guidance.
intent: How to learn from a Madhubani artist by studying the relationship between outline, repeated interior marks, filled space and subject choice rather than copying a whole style.

sources.title: Handicraft: Madhubani Painting
sources.publisher: District Administration, Madhubani, Government of Bihar
sources.purpose: Supports the regional name Mithila, line drawings with color and patterns, natural and mythological subjects, and the use of paper and cloth alongside wall painting.

sections.heading: Ask the artist where this painting belongs
paragraphs: Begin by asking the practitioner how they describe the work they teach: Madhubani, Mithila, or another term they prefer. The district administration describes Madhubani painting as Mithila art from the region and notes that its media now include paper, cloth and canvas as well as walls. Names and lineages matter, so let the artist locate their own practice.

A good first study can use one subject you know well: a bird, a plant from home, a family meal, or a small everyday scene. Ask whether the artist wants you to begin with a central figure or a border. The question of what to depict is part of the lesson because linework does not sit apart from the story.

sections.heading: Build the outline before filling it
paragraphs: The Madhubani district page describes line drawings filled with bright colors, contrasts or patterns. Watch how the artist decides the contour of a figure before adding decoration. On your own sheet, draw one large shape and leave enough room around it for the interior marks. A crowded outline makes it difficult to distinguish the subject from its ornament.

If the artist uses a bamboo-wrapped cotton brush or another tool, observe how the tip meets the paper and ask how pressure affects the line. Do not rush toward color to hide an uneven outline. Trace a simple contour once, then repeat it on the actual study. You are learning to direct the mark, not to imitate every flourish.

sections.heading: Use pattern to make each shape readable
paragraphs: Look at how repeated lines, dots, or small geometric marks fill an area without making every part identical. The district account says floral, animal, bird and geometric forms can help fill spaces in the painting. On your own bird, for example, you might give the body one repeated pattern and leave the wing divisions clearer. The choice should help a viewer read the form.

Ask the artist what a mark means in their own work before assigning it a symbolic meaning. A line that looks decorative to you may have a local name or a compositional purpose. Leave one patch of paper unfilled as a comparison, then decide with the artist whether the surrounding pattern should continue to the edge.

sections.heading: Keep color and contour in conversation
paragraphs: If the workshop includes pigment, ask whether you are using the artist’s prepared materials and what should be handled only by them. The Madhubani district page describes pigments and colors made by artists and notes that the colors in a traditional painting may be applied flat without shading. That observation can guide your choice: clear color blocks may suit a subject better than trying to model it with gradients.

Test one color in a small area and let it dry before adding the next. A consistent fill can make the silhouette feel stronger; a gap or bleed may reveal that the paper or tool is behaving differently than expected. Ask how the practitioner corrects an uneven edge. Follow their material-specific advice rather than applying generic watercolor techniques.

sections.heading: Make an original study rather than a copy
paragraphs: Use the artist’s instruction to make a scene that belongs to your own observation: a tree and the bird that visits it, a courtyard plant, or a meal set on a table. Borrow a technique you have been shown, such as a patterned border or a repeated interior line, while changing the subject and arrangement. Credit the practitioner if you later share the image.

Before leaving, ask the artist to point out one thing that works and one part to practise again. Record the medium, tool and one line-making detail in your notes. The next step might be drawing the same subject in a different shape or asking about how a particular motif is used, not announcing that one beginner exercise has captured an entire regional art tradition.
